PURPOSE
DIFFICULTY strand. The audit. This chapter is what makes the `what_the_car_cost` chapter credible.

MATERIAL ON HAND (verified; quotes are Kim's, verbatim in logs/proj_Smart_Car_log.md)
- THE PUMP IDENTITY: gallons x $/gal = cost. Three numbers that must multiply. 277 of 294 TwoRed rows balance; 143 of 170 Creamsicle US rows balance to under half a cent.
- The six instruments: pump identity, economy, geography (great-circle vs odometer), contiguity (repeated values in adjacent rows), price-family/same-pump, and the slashed zero.
- THE ERRATA ARCHITECTURE: corrections live BESIDE the source as a derived layer; the source is never edited; errata key to a ROW, never a LABEL. Reconstruct DISTANCES, never ODOMETER READINGS.
- Worked example: C01 Oxnard, where the $/gal cell is IDENTICAL to the gallons cell -- caught by contiguity, not by arithmetic.
- 65 TwoRed errata, 4 still open; 3 Creamsicle errata, all resolved.
- A field filled from a substitute source must record WHICH source: an AMEX merchant string is not a brand.

★★★ KIM'S STATEMENT, 2026-08-28 — VERBATIM. This is the chapter's thesis, in his words:
  "While this is a story about two cars, it is as much a story about data. Specifically the kind
   of data that's added now and then. Often under difficult conditions, like when you have cold,
   shivering hands. Or times when you're in a rush. It's easy to write down a wrong number.
   Transcription, too, often comes when you probably don't want to be typing a lot of numbers,
   some of which are hard to read. It is those distractions that can break the flow and cause
   another form of data error. The bottom line is that these types of data are difficult to get
   correct. When possible, enter fields that will let you cross check values (e.g., not just the
   date; add the day of the week)."
  ⚠ He says TWO cars, and for the data chapters that is right — TwoRed and Creamsicle carry the
    logs. Do not silently upgrade it to four.
  ★ TWO KINDS OF ERROR, and he separates them: the FIELD error (cold hands, haste) and the
    TRANSCRIPTION error (hard-to-read figures, broken flow). Different causes, different signatures.
    The Foreword now carries a short version of the first half; this chapter owns the full argument.
  → CH.9 OWNS THE LAST SENTENCE — the design lesson: **enter fields that let you cross check.**
    That is what every instrument in this chapter actually relies on, stated as advice.

★★★ AND IT HAS A WORKED EXAMPLE FOUND THE SAME DAY (2026-08-28) — the Creamsicle Ely row.
  - The date was written `2023-04-14`. It should be `2023-03-14` (Kim: an uncorrected typo).
  - NO instrument in the suite could see it. All six take the DATE as given (Finding 047).
  - What caught it was a REDUNDANT FIELD the log happens to carry: the odometer. Sorted by date,
    it ran backwards by 1,410 miles. **The odometer was acting as a second clock.**
  - ★ AND KIM'S OWN SUGGESTION WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT INSTANTLY, WITH NO ANALYSIS AT ALL:
    2023-04-14 was a **Friday**; 2023-03-14 was a **Tuesday**. A day-of-week column and the row
    contradicts itself on the page, at the moment of writing, where it is cheapest to fix.
  - THE ARGUMENT THIS MAKES: redundancy is not duplication. A cross-check field is a second,
    cheap measurement of the same event, and it is the only thing that can catch an error in a
    field every test trusts. **You cannot audit your way out of a missing column.**
  - ★★ AND IT DID CARRY A SECOND ERROR, IN THE CITY. The sheet said `Ely NV`; the receipts say
    `Las Vegas`. Caught by the geography instrument: Ely -> Beatty is 191 miles great-circle
    against 136 on the odometer, and **a great-circle distance is a floor** -- no road covers it.
    Corrected as C05. **TWO ERRORS IN ONE ROW, each invisible to every test but one, and each
    caught by a DIFFERENT redundant field** -- the odometer for the date, the map for the town.
  - ★★★ THE ENDING THE CHAPTER WANTED, AND KIM FOUND IT: **the fuel receipts print the odometer.**
    His words: *"a duplication of data I had forgotten about."* A FOURTH independent record, and
    the only one that duplicates the COUNTER -- the AMEX statements can settle gallons, price and
    merchant, never a counter reading. **So the cross-check field he recommends had been printing
    itself at the pump for years.** The advice is not only about designing the next sheet; half of
    it is FIND THE REDUNDANCY YOU ALREADY HAVE. That is a better close than the advice alone,
    and it ends in recovery rather than in a warning.
  - ⚠ THE INSTRUMENT HAS A FLOOR AND THE CHAPTER MUST SAY SO. Parowan -> Las Vegas reads 167
    odometer against 172 great-circle, ratio 0.97 -- also "impossible", and NOT a finding: a fill
    on the north-side I-15 corridor is ~12 miles closer and the ratio becomes 1.03. **A shortfall
    smaller than the spread of the city itself is coordinate imprecision.** 0.71 is not. Finding 036.
